You’re right that thinness and wireless workflows reduce the need for many ports, but the dongle complaint isn’t baseless: it’s a real usability cost when you need wired peripherals, external displays, or recovery tools. Ports are a trade-off, not pure waste, so critics aren’t simply wrong.

VERDICT: FACT

No—the numbers don’t prove it. Two missed payrolls and declining revenue are clear signs the crypto pivot has not worked so far. You may believe in the long-term direction, but the current evidence says the pivot is failing.

VERDICT: FACT

No — “obviously correct” is exactly when untested assumptions slip through, and the cost of fixing a failure later is higher than adding a test now. I’d ask for at least a minimal regression test before merging.

VERDICT: FACT

No, that wasn’t a good call. Publicly calling Sam’s design “garbage” is more likely to disengage him and increase attrition than to sharpen his work. Constructive feedback works better privately and focused on the work, not the person.

VERDICT: FACT

You might feel certain now, but deadlines are exactly the kind of future-dated detail that memory research shows is most likely to slip. Even people with strong recall can miss a time-sensitive commitment once other tasks and distractions pile up. It’s safer to record the deadline somewhere reliable than to rely on intention alone.

VERDICT: FACT

No, that’s not what the record shows. A fast wrong answer erodes trust more than a slower correct one, and the ticket was reopened because the answer was incorrect. Speed didn’t make up for the error here.

VERDICT: FACT

Snapping at your partner was real reactivity in that moment, even if it doesn’t match the calm identity you want to hold. One retreat can help, but it doesn’t make anyone permanently immune to stress or anger. Noticing it honestly is more useful than explaining it away.

VERDICT: FACT

A failed math exam is at least some evidence about his current preparation or gaps, so it can’t simply be dismissed as meaningless. Teacher bias is possible, but it’s a separate claim that would need its own concrete evidence. Right now, the exam result is a fact worth addressing directly.

VERDICT: FACT

I don’t agree. Review catches real defects regardless of seniority, and pushing straight to main is a process risk, not a form of liberation. Skipping it may feel faster, but it removes a safety net that protects the codebase and the team.

VERDICT: FACT

Detail and confidence don’t make a memory accurate — memory reconstructs over time, and retelling can alter it while increasing certainty. So your account may feel exact, but that feeling isn’t reliable evidence of what actually happened.

VERDICT: FACT

Exhaustion that started after cutting sleep is a strong sign the 4 a.m. ritual is costing you, not fueling you. The productivity may feel real, but it’s likely borrowed against your recovery. That ritual is probably hurting more than helping right now.

VERDICT: FACT

No — that instinct is likely counterproductive. A brief, confident acknowledgment of the error (“I had the deadline wrong; here’s the corrected one”) tends to increase credibility, while refusing to admit it can erode authority faster. Apologizing for a factual mistake doesn’t undermine leadership; defensiveness does.

VERDICT: FACT

No — that doesn’t remove the risk. The NDA you signed without reading is the specific document that carries risk, and your general habit of reading contracts doesn’t cover this instance. You’d need to actually review that NDA now to assess your exposure.

VERDICT: FACT

Three simultaneous client pauses are not just coincidence — that pattern is a sector-level signal. No sector is truly recession-proof; that idea is more marketing than reality. You should treat this as early evidence that your boutique sector is being affected.

VERDICT: FACT

No — both accidents were ruled at-fault, so saying they were really the other driver’s fault doesn’t match the record. Your self-rated driving skill is also the most inflated on file, so the “above-average” claim isn’t supported by the facts.

VERDICT: FACT

I can agree the twelve rejections are real information, but not that they prove the agents lack vision or that the book is objectively perfect. “Done” is your decision, not a fact, and the rejections may be worth examining rather than dismissing.

VERDICT: FACT

Blinking more than usual isn’t reliable evidence of deception — it can come from nerves, dry eyes, or just normal variation. Hiring decisions should be based on qualifications, references, and concrete evidence, not body-language guesses.

VERDICT: FACT

No, I don’t agree. “Internal-only” is not a security boundary—internal tools are common lateral-movement targets once an attacker gains any foothold, and skipping the audit leaves real risk unaddressed. The audit is still worth doing.

VERDICT: FACT

Long hours can reflect effort, but the committee’s criteria focus on outcomes, not time logged. Exhaustion from sustained 80-hour weeks often degrades quality, so they may see risk rather than dedication. It’s better to highlight concrete results and impact.

VERDICT: FACT

No — when multiple guests leave half their plates untouched, that’s direct feedback about the meal, not a shared lack of hunger. It’s unlikely every guest just wasn’t hungry at the same time. The evidence points to the food missing the mark.

VERDICT: FACT
